lessons.title: Water Needs at Different Growth Stages
lessons.body: Potatoes need different amounts of water at each stage of growth. Understanding these stages helps you avoid wasting water and ensure a healthy crop. The first stage is sprouting and emergence, from planting to when shoots appear. During this time, the soil should be moist but not soaked. Too much water can rot the seed potatoes. Light irrigation every 2-3 days is enough if the soil is dry. The second stage is vegetative growth, when leaves and stems grow quickly. Water needs increase. The plants need about 25-30 mm of water per week. In dry areas, you may need to irrigate twice a week. The third stage is tuber initiation, when the plant starts forming tubers. This is the most critical stage for water. Water stress now can reduce the number of tubers. Keep the soil evenly moist. The fourth stage is tuber bulking, when tubers grow in size. This is when the plant uses the most waterâabout 35-40 mm per week. Consistent moisture is key. If you let the soil dry out and then water heavily, tubers can crack. The fifth stage is maturation, when vines turn yellow and die back. Water needs drop. Reduce irrigation to avoid rotting tubers. Stop watering about 2 weeks before harvest. In Africa, where rainfall can be unpredictable, you may need to supplement with irrigation. A simple rain gauge (a tin can) can help you track rainfall. If you get less than 25 mm of rain in a week, you need to irrigate. Sandy soils drain quickly, so you may need to water more often but with less water each time. Clay soils hold water longer, so you can water less frequently. Always check soil moisture by digging 10 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, it's time to water. Remember, potatoes are shallow-rooted, so they need frequent, light watering rather than deep soaking. Overwatering can leach nutrients and cause disease. Underwatering reduces yield. Finding the balance is key to a successful crop.

lessons.title: Irrigation Systems: Drip, Sprinkler, Furrow
lessons.body: Choosing the right irrigation system for your potato farm depends on your budget, water source, and field size. The three main systems are drip, sprinkler, and furrow. Each has advantages and disadvantages. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the plant roots through pipes with small holes or emitters. It saves water because there is little evaporation. It also reduces weeds because only the crop gets water. Drip is good for small plots and areas with limited water. A basic drip kit for 100 square meters costs about $20-30. You can also make your own drip system using plastic bottles with small holes. However, drip lines can clog if water is dirty. You need to filter the water or clean the lines regularly. Sprinkler irrigation sprays water over the crop like rain. It is good for large fields and sandy soils. You can use hand-moved sprinklers or permanent systems. A simple hose-end sprinkler is cheap but uneven. A better option is a micro-sprinkler attached to a hose. Sprinklers can cause leaf diseases if leaves stay wet, so water early in the day so leaves dry before evening. Also, sprinklers lose water to evaporation in hot weather. Furrow irrigation is the oldest method. You dig small channels (furrows) between rows and let water flow. It is cheap and easy, but uses a lot of water. It can also cause soil erosion and waterlogging. Furrow is best for flat land with clay soil. For potatoes, raised beds with furrows on the sides work well. You can improve furrow by using surge flow or gated pipes. In Africa, many smallholders use furrow because it requires no special equipment. But if water is scarce, drip or sprinkler is better. Consider your water source: if you have a borehole with low yield, drip is ideal. If you have a river or dam, furrow or sprinkler may work. Also think about labour: drip and sprinkler need less labour after installation, while furrow needs someone to open and close channels. Whichever system you choose, make sure it applies water evenly. You can test by placing small cans around the field and measuring how much water each collects. Aim for uniform coverage.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Based on Soil Moisture
lessons.body: Scheduling irrigation means deciding when and how much to water. The best way is to check soil moisture. You don't need expensive tools. Your hand and a simple tensiometer can work. First, learn to feel soil moisture. Dig 10 cm into the soil near the plants. Squeeze a handful of soil. If it forms a ball and leaves a slight moisture film on your palm, it's moist enough. If it crumbles, it's too dry. If it drips water, it's too wet. For potatoes, you want the soil to feel like a wrung-out sponge. Check every 2-3 days during tuber bulking. A more precise tool is a tensiometer. It measures how hard plants must work to pull water from soil. You can buy one for $50-100. Install it at 15 cm depth. For potatoes, irrigate when the tensiometer reads 30-40 centibars (cb). If it reads above 60 cb, the crop is stressed. You can also use a simple soil moisture meter (about $10-20) that you push into the soil. It gives a reading from 1 (dry) to 10 (wet). Aim for 5-7. Another method is the feel and appearance method: take soil samples from several spots and compare to a chart. For sandy soil, irrigate when it feels dry at 10 cm. For clay, wait until it's slightly moist but not sticky. The amount to apply depends on soil type. Sandy soil holds little water, so apply 10-15 mm per irrigation. Clay holds more, so apply 20-25 mm. A simple way to measure water: use a hose with a known flow rate. For example, if your hose fills a 10-litre bucket in 30 seconds, that's 20 litres per minute. To apply 10 mm over 10 square meters, you need 100 litres. That would take 5 minutes. Keep a record of rainfall and irrigation. A notebook works. Write down date, amount, and crop stage. This helps you learn and adjust. In dry seasons, you may need to irrigate every 3-4 days. In rainy seasons, you may skip. Overwatering wastes water and leaches nutrients. Underwatering reduces yield. So scheduling is about balance. Start by checking soil moisture daily, then adjust to every 2-3 days as you gain experience.

lessons.title: Managing Drought Stress in Potatoes
lessons.body: Drought stress happens when potatoes don't get enough water. It can reduce yield by 50% or more. Potatoes are especially sensitive during tuber initiation and bulking. Signs of drought stress include wilting leaves in the morning, curling leaf edges, and dark green leaves. If you see these, act quickly. First, if you have irrigation, water immediately. But don't overwaterâapply a moderate amount and check soil moisture. If you have no irrigation, you can use mulching to conserve soil moisture. Spread dry grass, straw, or crop residues 5-10 cm thick around plants. This reduces evaporation by up to 70%. Mulch also keeps soil cool. Another method is to reduce plant spacing? No, that's not practical now. Instead, you can practice deficit irrigation: give less water but at critical stages. For example, if water is very scarce, prioritize tuber initiation and bulking. Skip irrigation during early vegetative growth if plants look healthy. You can also use shade nets if you grow high-value potatoes, but that's expensive. In Africa, many farmers rely on rain. If drought hits, you can try to harvest early if tubers are already formed. But immature tubers store poorly. Another strategy is to plant drought-tolerant varieties like 'Unica' or 'Cruza' if available. Also, improve soil organic matter by adding compost or manure. This helps soil hold water. A soil with 3% organic matter holds twice as much water as one with 1%. You can also dig small basins around plants to catch rain. If you have a water source but limited, use drip irrigation to maximize efficiency. During drought, avoid tilling the soil because it dries it out. Keep weeds downâthey compete for water. If you expect a long drought, consider reducing your planted area next season and focus water on a smaller plot. Finally, monitor weather forecasts. If rain is coming, you can wait. But don't wait too long. Potatoes can recover from short drought if watered before permanent wilting. After a drought, don't overwater suddenlyâthat can cause tuber cracking. Instead, water gradually over a few days. Remember, prevention is better: choose a field with good water-holding capacity, add organic matter, and irrigate before stress appears.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Salinity Issues
lessons.body: Not all water is good for potatoes. Water quality affects soil health and crop yield. The main concerns are salinity, sodicity, and contaminants. Salinity means water has high salt content. When you irrigate with salty water, salts build up in the soil. Potatoes are moderately sensitive to salinity. If soil salinity gets too high, plants wilt even when soil is wet, and yields drop. You can test water salinity with an electrical conductivity (EC) meter. A cheap handheld meter costs $20-50. For potatoes, water with EC above 1.5 dS/m can cause problems. If your water is salty, you can manage by leaching: apply extra water to push salts below the root zone. But this requires good drainage. Also, add gypsum if soil is sodic (high sodium). Another issue is water with high sodium. Sodium destroys soil structure, making it hard and less permeable. You can test with a simple kit. If sodium is high, avoid using that water. Contaminants include chemicals from upstream, sewage, or industrial waste. Never use water that smells bad or has visible oil or foam. In Africa, many farmers use river or dam water that may carry silt. Silt can clog drip lines. Let water settle in a tank before use. Also, water from shallow wells may be salty in coastal areas. If you suspect salinity, look for white crust on soil surface or stunted plants with dark green leaves. To manage salinity, plant salt-tolerant crops in rotation, like barley. Add organic matter to improve soil. Mulch to reduce evaporation that brings salts to surface. If salinity is severe, consider changing water source or installing drainage. For smallholders, rainwater harvesting is a good alternative. Collect roof runoff in tanks. This water is usually low in salts. Also, test your water before the season. Many agricultural extension offices offer low-cost water tests. If you can't test, observe your crop: if leaves are yellow between veins and plants are stunted, salinity might be the cause. Remember, prevention is easier than cure. Use the best water you can access.

lessons.title: Drainage and Avoiding Waterlogging
lessons.body: Potatoes hate waterlogged soil. Too much water suffocates roots, causes tuber rot, and reduces yield. Waterlogging happens when water cannot drain away after heavy rain or over-irrigation. Signs include yellowing leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, smelly tubers. To avoid this, ensure your field has good drainage. First, choose a field with a slope of 1-2% if possible. Flat land is more prone to waterlogging. If your land is flat, make raised beds. Raised beds are 20-30 cm high and 70-80 cm wide. They keep the root zone above the water table. You can make them with a hoe or a tractor. Second, dig drainage furrows between beds. These furrows should be 30 cm deep and lead to a lower area or a ditch. In heavy clay soil, you may need to install subsurface drainage. This involves burying perforated pipes 60-80 cm deep. It's expensive but effective. A cheaper option is to dig open ditches around the field. Third, improve soil structure by adding organic matter. Compost or manure helps clay soil drain better. Avoid working the soil when it's wetâthat compacts it and makes drainage worse. Fourth, manage irrigation carefully. Don't overwater. If you use furrow irrigation, make sure water doesn't stand in furrows for more than a few hours. For sprinkler, watch for runoff. If water runs off, reduce the application rate. Fifth, after heavy rain, check your field. If you see standing water, drain it quickly by opening channels. You can also plant on ridges to keep tubers above the water. In areas with high rainfall, plant on raised beds and use cover crops to improve soil. If you have a low spot, consider installing a French drain: a trench filled with gravel and a pipe. For small plots, you can dig a small pond to collect excess water. Remember, potatoes need oxygen in the soil. Waterlogging for even 24 hours can damage roots. So drainage is not optionalâit's essential. Plan it before planting. If you already have waterlogging, harvest early to save what you can. But prevention is better: test your soil drainage by digging a hole, filling it with water, and seeing how long it takes to drain. If it takes more than 24 hours, you need to improve drainage.

quiz.q: At which growth stage do potatoes need the most water?
quiz.explanation: Tuber bulking is when tubers grow in size and the plant uses the most water, about 35-40 mm per week.

quiz.q: How can you check if soil moisture is adequate for potatoes without tools?
options: A) Dig 10 cm and squeeze soil in your hand
D) Count the number of days since last rain
quiz.explanation: The feel method: if soil forms a ball and leaves slight moisture, it's moist enough.

quiz.q: What is a sign of drought stress in potatoes?
options: A) Wilting leaves in the morning
quiz.explanation: Wilting in the morning indicates the plant is losing water faster than it can take up.

quiz.q: Which irrigation system delivers water directly to plant roots and saves the most water?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation minimizes evaporation and runoff by applying water directly to the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of furrow irrigation?
options: B) Uses a lot of water
quiz.explanation: Furrow irrigation is cheap but uses more water than drip or sprinkler due to evaporation and deep percolation.

quiz.q: How often should you check soil moisture during tuber bulking?
quiz.explanation: During tuber bulking, water demand is high, so check every 2-3 days to avoid stress.

quiz.q: What does a tensiometer reading of 60 cb indicate for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: For potatoes, irrigate at 30-40 cb; above 60 cb means the crop is under water stress.

quiz.q: Which soil type requires more frequent but lighter irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil drains quickly and holds little water, so it needs more frequent, lighter applications.

quiz.q: What is a good way to conserve soil moisture during drought?
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces evaporation by up to 70% and keeps soil cool.

quiz.q: Which growth stage is most critical for water stress in potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Water stress during tuber initiation reduces the number of tubers formed.

quiz.q: What is deficit irrigation?
options: A) Applying less water than needed at all stages
C) Applying less water but prioritizing critical stages
quiz.explanation: Deficit irrigation means giving less water overall but ensuring critical stages like tuber initiation and bulking get enough.

quiz.q: How can you improve soil water-holding capacity?
quiz.explanation: Organic matter like compost or manure increases soil water-holding capacity.

quiz.q: What is a sign of salinity buildup in soil?
options: A) White crust on soil surface
quiz.explanation: White crust indicates salt accumulation, often from irrigating with salty water.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended EC of irrigation water for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes are moderately sensitive; water with EC above 1.5 dS/m can cause yield loss.

quiz.q: How can you manage salinity if your water is salty?
options: B) Leach with extra water and ensure drainage
quiz.explanation: Leaching pushes salts below the root zone, but requires good drainage.

quiz.q: What is a cheap way to test water salinity?
quiz.explanation: A handheld EC meter costs $20-50 and gives a reliable salinity reading.

quiz.q: Why is waterlogging bad for potatoes?
options: B) It suffocates roots and causes tuber rot
D) It makes soil too dry
quiz.explanation: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen, leading to root death and tuber rot.

quiz.q: What is a raised bed and why is it used?
options: B) A mound of soil that keeps roots above waterlogged conditions
quiz.explanation: Raised beds improve drainage and keep the root zone above the water table.

quiz.q: How deep should drainage furrows be?
quiz.explanation: Drainage furrows should be about 30 cm deep to carry excess water away.

quiz.q: What is a French drain?
options: B) A trench filled with gravel and a pipe
D) A tool for testing soil
quiz.explanation: A French drain collects and redirects subsurface water to prevent waterlogging.

quiz.q: How can you test if your soil has poor drainage?
options: A) Dig a hole, fill with water, and see how long it takes to drain
quiz.explanation: If water takes more than 24 hours to drain from a hole, drainage is poor.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching in potato farming?
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces evaporation and helps retain soil moisture.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is most suitable for a small plot with limited water?
quiz.explanation: Drip is water-efficient and ideal for small plots with scarce water.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of water per week for potatoes during vegetative growth?
quiz.explanation: During vegetative growth, potatoes need about 25-30 mm of water per week.

quiz.q: How can you reduce evaporation loss from sprinkler irrigation?
options: B) Irrigate early in the morning or evening
quiz.explanation: Irrigating during cooler parts of the day reduces evaporation losses.

quiz.q: What is a sign of overwatering in potatoes?
options: B) Yellowing leaves and soft tubers
quiz.explanation: Overwatering causes yellowing, root suffocation, and tuber rot.

quiz.q: Why is it important to stop irrigation before harvest?
options: B) To prevent tuber rot and allow skins to set
quiz.explanation: Stopping irrigation 2 weeks before harvest helps skins set and prevents rot.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to irrigate potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Early morning irrigation allows leaves to dry before evening, reducing disease risk.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure irrigation water amount?
options: B) A bucket and a watch
quiz.explanation: You can measure flow rate by timing how long it takes to fill a bucket of known volume.

quiz.q: What is the first step to manage drought stress?
quiz.explanation: If irrigation is available, water immediately to relieve stress.
